Capability model — parameter sensitivity

Cagliari · ELECTRE TRI-B capability classification · 1563 nodes · perturbation of the user-configured parameters. Figures are the percentage of nodes that change capability class unless stated otherwise. Read top to bottom: methodology, exact parameters tested, results section by section, then the conclusions at the end. Robustness to input noise is a separate report — see robustness_report.py.

1. How this analysis works

The model chain being tested

The model turns a location into a capability class through five steps, each carrying hand-set numbers that a human chose:

StepTurnsIntoGoverned byValues tested (below / above baseline)
① decaytravel timesper-mode reachabilitydecay_coefficient scaled by 0.8 (shorter travel tolerance) / scaled by 1.2 (longer travel tolerance)
② RRAmodal reachabilitiesper-POI accesslambda_mode (mode redundancy weights) every mode weighted equally (lambda=1) -- no redundancy discount / taper reversed -- the worst mode gets full weight, the best gets the smallest (design — pending rerun)
③ type aggregationper-POI accessper-POI-type valuecontribution_coefficient every POI type set to the minimum tier (1: saturates after 1 POI) / every POI type set to the maximum tier (8: needs 8 POIs to saturate)
④ ChoquetPOI-type values11 service scoreschoquet_capacity blended 50% toward uniform (less skewed) / deviations from uniform exaggerated 50% (more skewed)
choquet_interactions all defined pairs set to 0 (no interactions) / all defined pairs set to 0.7 (maximal interactions), sign preserved from baseline
⑤ ELECTRE TRI-Bservice scores3 capability classesq_factor 0.2, 0.25, 0.3
p_factor 0.65, 0.75, 0.85
λ cut 0.6, 0.65, 0.7

The question this report answers: are the chosen values in a stable region, or would small, defensible changes redraw the map? That is what lets a configuration be defended as the model rather than one of many arbitrary ones.

Sensitivity vs. robustness

Sensitivity (sections 4–5 here): do the parameters matter? Change a knob, measure how much the output moves. Identifies which numbers are load-bearing (need justification) vs decorative. A separate question, answered in its own report: robustness — is the output trustworthy given noisy inputs? Holds every parameter fixed and jitters the input service scores instead, to see how often a node keeps its class. A model can be insensitive to parameters yet non-robust to noise, or vice-versa — they are independent, which is why they get independent reports: see robustness_report.py (outputs/sensitivity/robustness_report.html).

How the numbers were produced (and why they are trustworthy)

Upstream parameters (decay, interactions, capacity, contribution) feed complex accessibility math, so they are not re-implemented. Each perturbation writes modified copies of the config CSVs and launches a fresh subprocess that runs the real accessibility + service stages from the cached travel times — the exact production code — so the results are about the real model. The original CSVs are backed up and hash-verified on restore, so a run can never leave your config mutated.

Downstream ELECTRE is pure arithmetic over the service scores, so it is vectorized for speed, then validated against the real electre_tri_integration() on sampled nodes before any analysis — the run aborts on any disagreement, so the fast path is provably the real model.

Metric glossary

MetricMeaning
% nodes changedFraction of nodes whose final capability class differs from baseline. A node counts only if it crosses a class boundary — so this measures decision changes, which is what matters for a map.
mean |score Δ|Average absolute change in the continuous score. Compared with "% changed" it shows why: many nodes flipped with a small Δ = they sat on a knife-edge.
mean |service Δ|Same, per individual service — traces which of the 11 services a perturbation actually moves.
node dropoutNodes that vanish because a parameter change leaves them with zero reachable POIs — itself a sensitivity signal.

Weight perturbation

Dirichlet draws around the configured (uniform) service weights, 200 draws per capability, concentration high enough that draws stay close to uniform (max single weight observed: 0.72).

Same data as a tornado plot per axis — the below-baseline config's effect extends left, the above-baseline config's extends right, one row per capability:

How to read it, axis by axis (worst-case % nodes changed, on whichever capability it hits hardest — verdict thresholds as in section 8):

  • decay_coefficient — load-bearing (40.0% on nutrition). travel-tolerance assumptions drive all three capabilities; it is also the only axis that changes which nodes exist (see dropout below).
  • contribution_coefficient — load-bearing (44.1% on care). every POI type is pinned to the minimum (1) or maximum (8) tier in the configured Fibonacci-like class set — the full range the modeler could plausibly have chosen.
  • choquet_capacity — load-bearing (23.9% on care). one direction flattens the hand-chosen skew toward uniform, the other exaggerates it 50% further — a genuine two-sided test of whether the exact weights matter.
  • choquet_interactions — load-bearing (86.4% on restorativeness). the baseline values are tiny (±0.03–0.07); this brackets a full order-of-magnitude range (0 vs 0.7 on every defined pair), so this verdict holds even under a generous swing, not just under the tiny configured range.

Where each perturbation acts — mean |service-score Δ| vs baseline (larger = that service moves more). This localizes the sensitivity: contribution changes concentrate in the diagnostic/rehabilitation services, while decay spreads across every service because it touches every POI type.

4. Downstream ELECTRE parameter sweeps (OAT)

One parameter at a time, all others at baseline, tested at exactly one value below and one value above baseline (section 2) — a direct local sensitivity check rather than a full curve. % of nodes changing class vs baseline (0% at baseline). The tornado plots below put the baseline value in the centre row; bars extend left for the below-baseline value and right for the above-baseline value, so an asymmetric shape (one side much longer than the other) is itself the finding — it means the model responds differently to tightening vs loosening that parameter right around its current value.

q_factor (baseline 0.25) — near-symmetric

Nudging q_factor one step either side of baseline moves at most ~3% of care, and both directions respond similarly: the baseline is not sitting on an edge.

λ cut level (baseline 0.65) — asymmetric

Even one step away, the two directions are not equal: moving to 0.70 flips up to 10% of care, markedly more than the equivalent step down to 0.60. λ is the credibility bar a location must clear to be promoted a class, and the model is visibly more sensitive on the high side right next to its current value — the single most consequential number in the model, and the one with the 0.65-vs-0.70 inconsistency flagged in the conclusions (section 8).

7. Why care is the fragile capability

Care is the most sensitive on every axis for compounding reasons:

  • It aggregates more services than the others, so it has more moving parts.
  • Its services include the longest travel-time tolerances (up to 45-minute half-times), so they are maximally exposed to the decay and contribution assumptions.
  • Empirically, its node scores cluster right at the class boundaries — so a small shift from any of the five stages tips many nodes across a boundary.

The through-line: care is not fragile because of one bad parameter — it is fragile because its scores live on the boundaries, and every parameter can push them over.

8. Conclusions

Ranked by how much they can move a capability's output, these are the parameters that most need an explicit justification. For every parameter tested, this takes the single worst % of nodes it can flip on any of the three capabilities (not just one) — that worst-case exposure is what should drive how much calibration effort a number gets, independent of which capability happens to show it.

Parameter influence ranking (most to least load-bearing)

Classified automatically at ≥20% = load-bearing, 5–20% = moderate, <5% = inert. "Worst-case %" is the largest effect seen on any capability; "hits hardest" names which one.

ParameterWorst-case % nodes changedHits hardestVerdict
choquet_interactions86.4%restorativenessload-bearing
ELECTRE service weights65.3%careload-bearing
contribution_coefficient44.1%careload-bearing
decay_coefficient40.0%nutritionload-bearing
choquet_capacity23.9%careload-bearing
lambda cut level18.6%restorativenessmoderate
p_factor4.3%careinert
q_factor3.2%careinert

Read: the load-bearing parameters at the top must be justified/calibrated for a stable model — they are the ones capable of redrawing the map on their own. The inert ones at the bottom can be set to any defensible value; tuning them is wasted effort.

The λ cut level is a cliff, and there is a bug on it. Moving λ off its baseline flips up to 10% of care nodes (see section 4) — the steepest response of any parameter, and the top of the ranking above. The code cuts at cred >= 0.65 (utils/capabilities.py) but the debug details report lambda_cut = 0.70; on the most consequential parameter in the model this 0.05 inconsistency alone moves ~10% of care nodes. Resolve it and pin λ with an explicit justification before treating any version as stable.

Where the load-bearing parameters actually bite

Care is the capability most exposed to parameter changes overall — averaged over every perturbation, its share of nodes changing class is: care (27.7%), restorativeness (21.8%), nutrition (20.2%). That is why it appears repeatedly as the "hits hardest" capability above: it is not that one parameter targets care specifically, but that its node scores sit right on the class boundaries (detailed in section 7), so whichever parameter turns out to be load-bearing tends to show its effect there first. Practically: when justifying a load-bearing parameter, check its effect on care first — that is where a bad choice will show up.

How much to trust the map

That is a separate question from everything above — parameter sensitivity says nothing about whether the output is robust to noise in the inputs. See the robustness report (robustness_report.py, outputs/sensitivity/robustness_report.html) for that analysis and its QGIS stability layer.

What to do for a stable parameter set

  1. Fix & pin λ — resolve the 0.65-vs-0.70 inconsistency and justify the value; it is the master knob.
  2. Calibrate the load-bearing upstream parameters (decay / contribution), especially for care's services.
  3. Freeze the inert parameters (interactions) at any defensible value — do not spend calibration effort there.
  4. Check the robustness report for which capabilities/nodes need to be presented with uncertainty.
  5. Leave q_factor / p_factor at baseline — they sit in proven-safe interior regions.
